advisors.name: Marine Carpuat
advisors.match_reason: Carpuat is the strongest match overall. Her group works directly on cross-lingual generalization and alignment in multilingual LLMs ("Can you map it to English? The role of cross-lingual alignment in the multilingual performance of LLMs"), speech-to-text quality estimation (SpeechQE on direct speech translation), and evaluation frameworks for AI-mediated communication that go beyond surface accuracy — all mapping tightly onto the applicant's interests in multilingual LLM adaptation, evaluation beyond translated benchmarks, and speech-text models. She also runs the CLIP Lab at UMD, the central hub for all NLP work at the department.

advisors.name: Rachel Rudinger
areas: Social and cultural fairness in AI
advisors.match_reason: Rudinger's research on "social and cultural fairness in AI" and evaluation methodology for LLMs aligns with the applicant's interest in evaluation that measures what matters for multilingual users — cultural grounding and fairness rather than translated English benchmarks. Her ACL 2025 paper (with Carpuat) on LLM agents debating for equitable cultural alignment is particularly relevant. However, her core focus is on commonsense reasoning and semantics in English, not low-resource multilingual adaptation or Indian languages specifically.

advisors.name: Sarah Wiegreffe
advisors.match_reason: Wiegreffe joined UMD CS in Fall 2025. Her expertise is in mechanistic interpretability and the faithfulness of natural language explanations — this touches the applicant's secondary interest in faithfulness evaluation. Her MIB benchmark (ICML 2025) and work on chain-of-thought monitorability could be relevant for understanding why multilingual models fail. However, her research has no direct connection to low-resource languages, Indian-language NLP, PEFT, or speech-text models.
